name: Nakanai
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.

new_statements.quote: p. 22: "Stress occurs on the penultimate syllable of the phrase, making it possible to distinguish affixes from separate particles." p. 256 (A4): "The phonological word in Nakanai is a rhythmic segment with nuclear stress on the penultimate syllable, and bounded by juncture." p. 256 (A4.1.1): "The distinguishing characteristic of the nuclear syllable is primary pitch. Primary intensity occurs on the first syllable. Thus primary pitch and primary intensity co-occur in two-syllable phonological words." p. 248 (A2.1): "(stress being predictable on the penultimate syllable - see section A4.1.)"

On the nuclear syllable of a pause group intensity and intonation peak simultaneously on the penultimate syllable of the final word (see 3.1.2.0.)' verbatim. p. 248 (PDF 262): '(stress being predictable on the penultimate syllable - see section A4.1.)' verbatim;…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (penultimate stress = penultimate): agrees on penultimate stress and adds the domain (phonological word / phrase-final word of the pause group), the pitch-vs-intensity split, and the listed exceptions (intensifier -o, deictics -e/-o, clipped forms, ten unstressed monosyllabic function words). Describes the Bileki (western, Cape Hoskins) dialect.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (primary pitch, the 'nucleus') falls predictably on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word; at phrase level the intonation peak coincides with the penultimate syllable of the last word of the pause group. Stress is described as increased intensity on the penult of each separate word, and it is used as the criterion for distinguishing affixes (inside the word, shifting stress) from separate particles.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress as such is described; Johnston separates two cues: primary pitch marks the nuclear (penultimate) syllable, while primary intensity falls on the first syllable of the phonological word (A4.1.1-A4.1.2, p. 256), so an initial intensity peak accompanies the penultimate pitch peak in words of three or more syllables. Elsewhere (p. 180) stress is said to consist 'mainly of increased intensity on the penultimate syllable of each separate word'.
new_statements.exceptions: (a) The intensifier suffix -o does not attract stress: stress 'remains static' (alalavi 'yesterday' -> alalavio 'day before yesterday', stress unchanged), A4.2.2.1, p. 257. (b) With the deictic particles -e 'here' and -o 'there' stress 'may shift to the final syllable, or remain static, instead of shifting to the penultimate syllable' (poue [pou'e] 'sit here', poloo [polo'o] 'follow there'), A4.2.2.2, p. 257. (c) Shortened forms keep the old stress: isasa [i'sasa] 'one' -> isa [i'sa] with no shift to the penult; gomai -> [go'ma]; A4.2.3, p. 258. (d) Ten monosyllabic grammatically dependent words (noun markers la, e; possessor te; conjunctions me, o, le; aspect markers ga, ge, so, ka) lack penultimate stress and bind rhythmically to the following word, A4.2.4, p. 258. (e) At phrase level the tag-question marker carries the stress nucleus finally with rising intonation (sec. 3.1.2, p. 69-70), and 'hesitation and calling' contours are exceptions to the penultimate nucleus (sec. 3.1.2.0, p. 67).
new_statements.identity_note: Both on-disk sources describe the Bileki dialect of Nakanai (Johnston 1980, p. 8: 'the present study is based on fieldwork in the Bileki dialect'; Chowning & Goodenough 2016, p. i: 'This dictionary represents the Bileki dialect.. of the Hoskins Peninsula'). Bileki is the principal/westernmost dialect; the other dialects (Ubae, Vele, Loso, Maututu) are not covered by any stress statement found.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (Nakanai fixed-dominant penultimate stress = penult) and word-for-word the same sentence as Johnston 1980 PL B-70 p. 22 already held by the project ('Stress occurs on the penultimate syllable of the phrase, making it possible to distinguish affixes from separate particles'); the OPD (data checked by Johnston 1992) adds nothing beyond Johnston 1980 except confirming the dialect (Bileki) and the phrase as domain.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable; the OPD states the domain as the (phonological) phrase, so a word plus following clitic particles is stressed on the penult of the whole group, which is used as a diagnostic separating affixes from free particles. No tone or contrastive length is reported (the suprasegmentals section contains only this stress sentence).
new_statements.exceptions: none stated as exceptions; the phonological conventions note optional non-pronunciation of word-final /i/ after /t/,/s/ and of final /u/ after /m/ (e.g. /e latumu/ [e l'tum]), which can make surface stress appear final, but the OPD does not discuss this as a stress exception
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD describes the Bileki dialect of Nakanai (Lakalai), Cape Hoskins, West New Britain Province [NAK] = naka1262; village list Waisissi.. Baikahea; same dialect as Johnston 1980 and the catalog record.

audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-dominant penultimate, not strict) rests on the standard reference grammar (Johnston 1980, PL B-70, 310 pp.) with a phonology appendix; both quoted sentences were confirmed verbatim in the now-saved open PDF (pp.256 and 180), and the grammar's own listed exceptions (enclitic deictics, intensifier -o, a handful of final-stressed words) justify 'dominant' rather than 'strict'. Glottolog lists no other grammar or phonology for naka1262, and the only later substantial work found (Chowning & Goodenough 2016 dictionary, downloaded) is silent on stress placement. Only housekeeping: the locator should read 'sect. 6.3 p.180 and App. A4 p.256' rather than '3.1.2, A4', and the record could note Johnston's remark that the penult nucleus is cued by pitch with intensity word-initial (A4.1.1).

sources.citation: Chowning, Ann & Ward H. Goodenough. 2016. A dictionary of the Lakalai (Nakanai) language of New Britain, Papua New Guinea. Asia-Pacific Linguistics A-PL 29. Canberra: ANU. 421 pp. (open, hdl.handle.net/1885/107217)
sources.quote: No explicit stress-placement rule; only stress-conditioned processes ('Vowels are usually lengthened slightly when stressed'; /au/ > /o/ 'if the immediately following syllable has primary stress'; vowel drop in CVCV when 'stress falls on the second of the two vowels', e.g. alalavi > allavi). One lexical note: interrogative particle ia 'stressed on last syllable'.
sources.note: No placement rule is given; the stress-conditioned examples (allavi from alalavi 'yesterday' with stress on the second of two like vowels; la-molavi from la-maulavi with primary stress on the following syllable) are consistent with penultimate stress but the work does not say so. Describes the Bileki dialect (Galilo village, eastern Hoskins Peninsula).
